Appendix A Linear rank-1 RNN

We provide here a complete derivation of the linear rank-1 RNN, including both the within-episode dynamics and the across-episode learning dynamics.

A.1 Within-episode dynamics

With rank-1 connectivity 𝑾=1N​𝒖​𝒗⊤\bm{W}=\frac{1}{N}\bm{u}\bm{v}^{\top} and linear activation ϕ=id\phi=\mathrm{id}, the state dynamics becomes

𝒉˙​(t)=−𝒉⁡(t)+1N​𝒖​𝒗⊤​𝒉​(t)+𝒎​x​(t)\dot{\bm{h}}(t)=-\bm{h}(t)+\frac{1}{N}\bm{u}\bm{v}^{\top}\bm{h}(t)+\bm{m}\,x(t) (A.1)

Assuming 𝒉⁡(0)=𝟎\bm{h}(0)=\bm{0}, the right-hand side of Eq. (A.1) always lies in span​{𝒎,𝒖}\mathrm{span}\{\bm{m},\bm{u}\}, since

𝒖​𝒗⊤​𝒉​(t)∈span⁡{𝒖}and𝒎​x​(t)∈span⁡{𝒎}\bm{u}\bm{v}^{\top}\bm{h}(t)\in\mathrm{span}\{\bm{u}\}\quad\text{and}\quad\bm{m}\,x(t)\in\mathrm{span}\{\bm{m}\}\quad

Therefore 𝒉⁡(t)∈span​{𝒎,𝒖}\bm{h}(t)\in\mathrm{span}\{\bm{m},\bm{u}\} for all tt, and we may write

𝒉⁡(t)=κm​(t)​𝒎+κu​(t)​𝒖,𝜿⁡(t)=[κm​(t)κu​(t)]∈ℝ2\bm{h}(t)=\kappa_{m}(t)\,\bm{m}+\kappa_{u}(t)\,\bm{u},\qquad\bm{\kappa}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}\kappa_{m}(t)\\[2.0pt] \kappa_{u}(t)\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{2} (A.2)

Projecting Eq. (A.1) onto this subspace yields the effective dynamics

𝜿˙​(t)=−𝜿⁡(t)+[001N​𝒗⊤​𝒎1N​𝒗⊤​𝒖]​𝜿​(t)+[10]​x​(t)\dot{\bm{\kappa}}(t)=-\bm{\kappa}(t)+\begin{bmatrix}0&0\\ \tfrac{1}{N}\bm{v}^{\top}\bm{m}&\tfrac{1}{N}\bm{v}^{\top}\bm{u}\end{bmatrix}\bm{\kappa}(t)+\begin{bmatrix}1\\[2.0pt] 0\end{bmatrix}x(t) (A.3)

and readout

y^​(t)=1N​𝒛⊤​𝒉​(t)=1N​[𝒛⊤​𝒎𝒛⊤​𝒖]​𝜿​(t)\hat{y}(t)=\frac{1}{N}\bm{z}^{\top}\bm{h}(t)=\frac{1}{N}\begin{bmatrix}\bm{z}^{\top}\bm{m}&\bm{z}^{\top}\bm{u}\end{bmatrix}\bm{\kappa}(t) (A.4)

A.2 Across-episode learning dynamics

The episode loss depends on the parameters only through the loss-visible overlaps

ℒ=ℒ⁡(σz​m,σz​u,σv​m,σv​u)\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}\bigl(\sigma_{zm},\sigma_{zu},\sigma_{vm},\sigma_{vu}\bigr) (A.5)

By the chain rule, the gradients with respect to the parameter vectors can be written as

∂ℒ∂𝒎\displaystyle\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\bm{m}} =∂ℒ∂σz​m​∂σz​m∂𝒎+∂ℒ∂σv​m​∂σv​m∂𝒎=1N​(∇z​m𝒛+∇v​m𝒗)\displaystyle=\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\sigma_{zm}}\frac{\partial\sigma_{zm}}{\partial\bm{m}}+\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\sigma_{vm}}\frac{\partial\sigma_{vm}}{\partial\bm{m}}=\frac{1}{N}\left(\nabla_{zm}\bm{z}+\nabla_{vm}\bm{v}\right) (A.6)
∂ℒ∂𝒖\displaystyle\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\bm{u}} =∂ℒ∂σz​u​∂σz​u∂𝒖+∂ℒ∂σv​u​∂σv​u∂𝒖=1N​(∇z​u𝒛+∇v​u𝒗)\displaystyle=\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\sigma_{zu}}\frac{\partial\sigma_{zu}}{\partial\bm{u}}+\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\sigma_{vu}}\frac{\partial\sigma_{vu}}{\partial\bm{u}}=\frac{1}{N}\left(\nabla_{zu}\bm{z}+\nabla_{vu}\bm{v}\right) (A.7)
∂ℒ∂𝒗\displaystyle\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\bm{v}} =∂ℒ∂σv​m​∂σv​m∂𝒗+∂ℒ∂σv​u​∂σv​u∂𝒗=1N​(∇v​m𝒎+∇v​u𝒖)\displaystyle=\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\sigma_{vm}}\frac{\partial\sigma_{vm}}{\partial\bm{v}}+\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\sigma_{vu}}\frac{\partial\sigma_{vu}}{\partial\bm{v}}=\frac{1}{N}\left(\nabla_{vm}\bm{m}+\nabla_{vu}\bm{u}\right) (A.8)
∂ℒ∂𝒛\displaystyle\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\bm{z}} =∂ℒ∂σz​m​∂σz​m∂𝒛+∂ℒ∂σz​u​∂σz​u∂𝒛=1N​(∇z​m𝒎+∇z​u𝒖)\displaystyle=\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\sigma_{zm}}\frac{\partial\sigma_{zm}}{\partial\bm{z}}+\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\sigma_{zu}}\frac{\partial\sigma_{zu}}{\partial\bm{z}}=\frac{1}{N}\left(\nabla_{zm}\bm{m}+\nabla_{zu}\bm{u}\right) (A.9)

Under gradient flow, 𝜽˙=−∇𝜽ℒ\dot{\bm{\theta}}=-\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}\mathcal{L}, the parameter dynamics become

𝒎˙\displaystyle\dot{\bm{m}} =−N−1​(∇z​m𝒛+∇v​m𝒗)𝒖˙=−N−1​(∇z​u𝒛+∇v​u𝒗)\displaystyle=-{N}^{-1}(\nabla_{zm}\,\bm{z}+\nabla_{vm}\,\bm{v})\,\,\qquad\dot{\bm{u}}=-{N}^{-1}(\nabla_{zu}\,\bm{z}+\nabla_{vu}\,\bm{v}) (A.10)
𝒗˙\displaystyle\dot{\bm{v}} =−N−1​(∇v​m𝒎+∇v​u𝒖)𝒛˙=−N−1​(∇z​m𝒎+∇z​u𝒖)\displaystyle=-{N}^{-1}(\nabla_{vm}\,\bm{m}+\nabla_{vu}\,\bm{u})\qquad\dot{\bm{z}}=-{N}^{-1}(\nabla_{zm}\,\bm{m}+\nabla_{zu}\,\bm{u})

By the product rule, for any two vectors 𝒗\bm{v} and 𝒖\bm{u}, the derivative of their inner product is

dd​τ​(𝒗⊤​𝒖)=𝒗˙⊤​𝒖+𝒗⊤​𝒖˙\frac{d}{d\tau}(\bm{v}^{\top}\bm{u})=\dot{\bm{v}}^{\top}\bm{u}+\bm{v}^{\top}\dot{\bm{u}} (A.11)

Applying this to the loss-visible overlaps together with Eq. (A.10) yields the induced dynamics

σ˙z​m\displaystyle\dot{\sigma}_{zm} =−(‖𝒎‖2+‖𝒛‖2)​∇z​m−σm​u​∇z​u−σz​v​∇v​m\displaystyle=-(\|\bm{m}\|^{2}+\|\bm{z}\|^{2})\nabla_{zm}-\sigma_{mu}\nabla_{zu}-\sigma_{zv}\nabla_{vm} (A.12)
σ˙z​u\displaystyle\dot{\sigma}_{zu} =−σm​u​∇z​m−(‖𝒖‖2+‖𝒛‖2)​∇z​u−σz​v​∇v​u\displaystyle=-\sigma_{mu}\nabla_{zm}-(\|\bm{u}\|^{2}+\|\bm{z}\|^{2})\nabla_{zu}-\sigma_{zv}\nabla_{vu}
σ˙v​m\displaystyle\dot{\sigma}_{vm} =−(‖𝒎‖2+‖𝒗‖2)​∇v​m−σm​u​∇v​u−σz​v​∇z​m\displaystyle=-(\|\bm{m}\|^{2}+\|\bm{v}\|^{2})\nabla_{vm}-\sigma_{mu}\nabla_{vu}-\sigma_{zv}\nabla_{zm}
σ˙v​u\displaystyle\dot{\sigma}_{vu} =−σm​u​∇v​m−(‖𝒖‖2+‖𝒗‖2)​∇v​u−σz​v​∇z​u\displaystyle=-\sigma_{mu}\nabla_{vm}-(\|\bm{u}\|^{2}+\|\bm{v}\|^{2})\nabla_{vu}-\sigma_{zv}\nabla_{zu}

which revealed six additional loss-invisible overlaps that are needed to close the learning dynamics

σm​u,σz​v,‖𝒎‖2,‖𝒖‖2,‖𝒗‖2,‖𝒛‖2\sigma_{mu},\quad\sigma_{zv},\quad\|\bm{m}\|^{2},\quad\ \|\bm{u}\|^{2},\quad\ \|\bm{v}\|^{2},\quad\ \|\bm{z}\|^{2} (A.13)

Similarly, their evolution under gradient flow is

σ˙m​u\displaystyle\dot{\sigma}_{mu} =−σz​u​∇z​m−σz​m​∇z​u−σv​u​∇v​m−σv​m​∇v​u\displaystyle=-\sigma_{zu}\nabla_{zm}-\sigma_{zm}\nabla_{zu}-\sigma_{vu}\nabla_{vm}-\sigma_{vm}\nabla_{vu} (A.14)
σ˙z​v\displaystyle\dot{\sigma}_{zv} =−σv​m​∇z​m−σv​u​∇z​u−σz​m​∇v​m−σz​u​∇v​u\displaystyle=-\sigma_{vm}\nabla_{zm}-\sigma_{vu}\nabla_{zu}-\sigma_{zm}\nabla_{vm}-\sigma_{zu}\nabla_{vu}
‖𝒎‖2˙\displaystyle\dot{\|\bm{m}\|^{2}} =−2​(σz​m​∇z​m+σv​m​∇v​m)\displaystyle=-2(\sigma_{zm}\nabla_{zm}+\sigma_{vm}\nabla_{vm})
‖𝒖‖2˙\displaystyle\dot{\|\bm{u}\|^{2}} =−2​(σz​u​∇z​u+σv​u​∇v​u)\displaystyle=-2(\sigma_{zu}\nabla_{zu}+\sigma_{vu}\nabla_{vu})
‖𝒗‖2˙\displaystyle\dot{\|\bm{v}\|^{2}} =−2​(σv​m​∇v​m+σv​u​∇v​u)\displaystyle=-2(\sigma_{vm}\nabla_{vm}+\sigma_{vu}\nabla_{vu})
‖𝒛‖2˙\displaystyle\dot{\|\bm{z}\|^{2}} =−2​(σz​m​∇z​m+σz​u​∇z​u)\displaystyle=-2(\sigma_{zm}\nabla_{zm}+\sigma_{zu}\nabla_{zu})

These equations form a closed 1010-dimensional ODE system in scalar variables, which fully describes the learning trajectory in overlap space.

A.3 Learning dynamics in matrix form

The learning dynamics can be written compactly in matrix form by defining

𝜽=[𝒎𝒖𝒗𝒛]∈ℝ4​N,𝝈=[σz​mσz​uσv​mσv​u]∈ℝ4,∇𝝈ℒ=∂ℒ∂𝝈=[∇z​m∇z​u∇v​m∇v​u]∈ℝ4\bm{\theta}=\begin{bmatrix}\bm{m}\\[2.0pt] \bm{u}\\[2.0pt] \bm{v}\\[2.0pt] \bm{z}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{4N},\qquad\bm{\sigma}=\begin{bmatrix}\sigma_{zm}\\[2.0pt] \sigma_{zu}\\[2.0pt] \sigma_{vm}\\[2.0pt] \sigma_{vu}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{4},\qquad\nabla_{\bm{\sigma}}\mathcal{L}=\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\bm{\sigma}}=\begin{bmatrix}\nabla_{zm}\\[2.0pt] \nabla_{zu}\\[2.0pt] \nabla_{vm}\\[2.0pt] \nabla_{vu}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{4} (A.15)

Let 𝑫\bm{D} denote the Jacobian of the overlap map with respect to the parameters

𝑫⁡(𝜽)=∂𝝈∂𝜽=1N​[𝒛⊤00𝒎⊤0𝒛⊤0𝒖⊤𝒗⊤0𝒎⊤00𝒗⊤𝒖⊤0]∈ℝ4×4​N\bm{D}(\bm{\theta})=\frac{\partial\bm{\sigma}}{\partial\bm{\theta}}=\frac{1}{N}\begin{bmatrix}\bm{z}^{\top}&0&0&\bm{m}^{\top}\\ 0&\bm{z}^{\top}&0&\bm{u}^{\top}\\ \bm{v}^{\top}&0&\bm{m}^{\top}&0\\ 0&\bm{v}^{\top}&\bm{u}^{\top}&0\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{4\times 4N} (A.16)

Under gradient flow, 𝜽˙=−𝑫​(𝜽)⊤​∇𝝈ℒ\dot{\bm{\theta}}=-\bm{D}(\bm{\theta})^{\top}\nabla_{\bm{\sigma}}\mathcal{L}, and the induced overlap dynamics follow as

𝝈˙=𝑫⁡(𝜽)​𝜽˙=−𝑫⁡(𝜽)​𝑫​(𝜽)⊤​∇𝝈ℒ=−𝑮⁡(𝜽)​∇𝝈ℒ,𝑮⁡(𝜽)=𝑫⁡(𝜽)​𝑫​(𝜽)⊤\dot{\bm{\sigma}}=\bm{D}(\bm{\theta})\,\dot{\bm{\theta}}=-\bm{D}(\bm{\theta})\bm{D}(\bm{\theta})^{\top}\,\nabla_{\bm{\sigma}}\mathcal{L}=-\bm{G}(\bm{\theta})\,\nabla_{\bm{\sigma}}\mathcal{L},\qquad\bm{G}(\bm{\theta})=\bm{D}(\bm{\theta})\bm{D}(\bm{\theta})^{\top} (A.17)

The matrix 𝑮⁡(𝜽)\bm{G}(\bm{\theta}) is given explicitly by

𝑮⁡(𝜽)=1N​[‖𝒎‖2+‖𝒛‖2σm​uσz​v0σm​u‖𝒖‖2+‖𝒛‖20σz​vσz​v0‖𝒎‖2+‖𝒗‖2σm​u0σz​vσm​u‖𝒖‖2+‖𝒗‖2]∈ℝ4×4\bm{G}(\bm{\theta})=\frac{1}{N}\begin{bmatrix}\|\bm{m}\|^{2}+\|\bm{z}\|^{2}&\sigma_{mu}&\sigma_{zv}&0\\ \sigma_{mu}&\|\bm{u}\|^{2}+\|\bm{z}\|^{2}&0&\sigma_{zv}\\ \sigma_{zv}&0&\|\bm{m}\|^{2}+\|\bm{v}\|^{2}&\sigma_{mu}\\ 0&\sigma_{zv}&\sigma_{mu}&\|\bm{u}\|^{2}+\|\bm{v}\|^{2}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{4\times 4} (A.18)

The dynamics of the loss-invisible overlaps can be written in an analogous matrix form. Define

𝝈~=(σm​u,σz​v,‖𝒎‖2,‖𝒖‖2,‖𝒗‖2,‖𝒛‖2)⊤,𝑫⁡(θ)~=∂𝝈~∂𝜽\tilde{\bm{\sigma}}=\begin{pmatrix}\sigma_{mu},\,\sigma_{zv},\,\|\bm{m}\|^{2},\,\|\bm{u}\|^{2},\,\|\bm{v}\|^{2},\,\|\bm{z}\|^{2}\end{pmatrix}^{\!\top},\quad\tilde{\bm{D}(\theta)}=\frac{\partial\tilde{\bm{\sigma}}}{\partial\bm{\theta}} (A.19)

Using 𝜽˙=−𝑫⊤​(𝜽)​∇𝝈ℒ\dot{\bm{\theta}}=-\bm{D}^{\top}(\bm{\theta})\nabla_{\bm{\sigma}}\mathcal{L}, the induced dynamics of 𝝈~\tilde{\bm{\sigma}} follow as

𝝈~˙=−𝑫~​(𝜽)​𝑫​(𝜽)⊤​∇𝝈ℒ=−𝑮~​(𝜽)​∇𝝈ℒ,𝑮~​(𝜽)=𝑫~​(𝜽)​𝑫⊤​(𝜽)\dot{\tilde{\bm{\sigma}}}=-\tilde{\bm{D}}(\bm{\theta})\bm{D}(\bm{\theta})^{\top}\,\nabla_{\bm{\sigma}}\mathcal{L}=-\tilde{\bm{G}}(\bm{\theta})\,\nabla_{\bm{\sigma}}\mathcal{L},\qquad\tilde{\bm{G}}(\bm{\theta})=\tilde{\bm{D}}(\bm{\theta})\bm{D}^{\top}(\bm{\theta}) (A.20)

With 𝑮⁡(𝜽)~\tilde{\bm{G}(\bm{\theta})} given explicitly as

𝑮~​(𝜽)=1N​[σz​uσz​mσv​uσv​mσv​mσv​uσz​mσz​u2​σz​m02​σv​m002​σz​u02​σv​u002​σv​m2​σv​u2​σz​m2​σz​u00]∈ℝ6×4\tilde{\bm{G}}(\bm{\theta})=\frac{1}{N}\begin{bmatrix}\sigma_{zu}&\sigma_{zm}&\sigma_{vu}&\sigma_{vm}\\ \sigma_{vm}&\sigma_{vu}&\sigma_{zm}&\sigma_{zu}\\ 2\sigma_{zm}&0&2\sigma_{vm}&0\\ 0&2\sigma_{zu}&0&2\sigma_{vu}\\ 0&0&2\sigma_{vm}&2\sigma_{vu}\\ 2\sigma_{zm}&2\sigma_{zu}&0&0\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{6\times 4} (A.21)

That is, the learning dynamics reduce to a closed 10D coupled ODE system

𝝈˙=−𝑮⁡(𝜽)​∇𝝈ℒ,𝝈~˙=−𝑮~​(𝜽)​∇𝝈ℒ\dot{\bm{\sigma}}=-\bm{G}(\bm{\theta})\,\nabla_{\bm{\sigma}}\mathcal{L},\qquad\dot{\tilde{\bm{\sigma}}}=-\tilde{\bm{G}}(\bm{\theta})\,\nabla_{\bm{\sigma}}\mathcal{L} (A.22)

which translates parameter-space learning dynamics into overlap-space learning. For a complete treatment, we derive the augmented 10×1010\times 10 Gram matrix 𝑮¯\bar{\bm{G}} in App. C.

A.4 Filter task

As a concrete example for the rank-1 linear RNN, we consider the simple task of reproducing a first-order exponential filter driven by white-noise input [25] (Fig. 5). The transfer function defines the target response

y⋆(t)=a⋆e−c⋆​t∗x(t)⟺H⋆(s)=a⋆s+c⋆y^{\star}(t)=a^{\star}\,e^{-c^{\star}t}*x(t)\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad H^{\star}(s)=\frac{a^{\star}}{s+c^{\star}} (A.23)

where x⁡(t)x(t) denotes a white-noise input signal, a⋆a^{\star} is the filter gain, c⋆>0c^{\star}>0 is the decay rate, and y⋆​(t)y^{\star}(t) is the target.

A.4.1 Training details and RNN initialization

Numerical simulations were performed by training a continuous-time rank-1 RNN discretized via the Euler method (Δ​t=0.025\Delta t=0.025) and size N=500N=500. Every element of the trainable vectors 𝜽={𝒎,𝒖,𝒗,𝒛}⊂ℝN\bm{\theta}=\{\bm{m},\bm{u},\bm{v},\bm{z}\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{N} is initialized i.i.d. from a standard normal distribution 𝒩⁡(0,1)\mathcal{N}(0,1). Training is performed by gradient descent with learning rate η=5×10−3\eta=5\times 10^{-3} to match the filter target with gain a⋆=1a^{\star}=1 and decay rate c⋆=0.2c^{\star}=0.2, using the impulse (delta) response as input, and for an episode of length T=20​sT=20\,\mathrm{s}. The loss is the time-integrated squared error between the network output and the target. For the A–B–A training protocol, task A filter parameters are as described above, while task B uses the same gain a⋆=1a^{\star}=1 but a different decay rate c⋆=0.4c^{\star}=0.4. In the same protocol, during the noisy training phase, Gaussian noise 𝒩⁡(0,0.01)\mathcal{N}(0,0.01) is added to the target labels (Fig. 7).

A.4.2 Network impulse response and exact solution

For the effective 2D RNN described in Eqs. (A.3), (A.4), the impulse response can be obtained in closed form. Define

A=[−10σv​m−1+σv​u],B=[10],C=[σz​mσz​u]A=\begin{bmatrix}-1&0\\ \sigma_{vm}&-1+\sigma_{vu}\end{bmatrix},\qquad B=\begin{bmatrix}1\\ 0\end{bmatrix},\qquad C=\begin{bmatrix}\sigma_{zm}&\sigma_{zu}\end{bmatrix} (A.24)

The Laplace transform of the transfer function from the input xx to the output y^\hat{y} reads

H⁡(s)=C​(s​I−A)−1​B=s​σz​m+σv​m​σz​u−σv​u​σz​m+σz​m(s+1)​(s+1−σv​u)H(s)=C(sI-A)^{-1}B=\frac{s\,\sigma_{zm}+\sigma_{vm}\sigma_{zu}-\sigma_{vu}\sigma_{zm}+\sigma_{zm}}{(s+1)(s+1-\sigma_{vu})} (A.25)

and the corresponding impulse response (kernel) is a sum of two exponentials

(σz​m−σz​u​σv​mσv​u)​e−t+σz​u​σv​mσv​u​e−(1−σv​u)​t\Big(\sigma_{zm}-\frac{\sigma_{zu}\sigma_{vm}}{\sigma_{vu}}\Big)e^{-t}\;+\;\frac{\sigma_{zu}\sigma_{vm}}{\sigma_{vu}}\,e^{-(1-\sigma_{vu})t} (A.26)

To match the target one–pole filter a⋆​e−c⋆​ta^{\star}e^{-c^{\star}t} exactly, the unwanted e−te^{-t} mode must vanish, and the remaining pole and amplitude must be set to c⋆c^{\star} and a⋆a^{\star}, respectively. This yields the following constraints

σv​u=1−c⋆,σz​u​σv​mσv​u=a⋆,σz​m=a⋆\sigma_{vu}=1-c^{\star},\qquad\frac{\sigma_{zu}\sigma_{vm}}{\sigma_{vu}}=a^{\star},\qquad\sigma_{zm}=a^{\star} (A.27)

Notably, this expression depends on σz​u\sigma_{zu} and σv​m\sigma_{vm} only through their product, implying a continuous rescaling symmetry σz​u→α​σz​u,σv​m→α−1​σv​m\sigma_{zu}\!\to\!\alpha\,\sigma_{zu},\;\sigma_{vm}\!\to\!\alpha^{-1}\sigma_{vm} under which the network function is invariant. This further mean, that any pair (σz​u,σv​m)(\sigma_{zu},\sigma_{vm}) satisfying the product constraint σz​u​σv​m=a⋆​(1−c⋆)\sigma_{zu}\sigma_{vm}=a^{\star}(1-c^{\star}) provides a valid solution. These constraints reveal a 1D degenerate manifold of global minima in the visible overlap space. Within this manifold, we identify the balanced solution as the unique symmetric point where

σz​u=σv​m=a⋆​(1−c⋆)\sigma_{zu}=\sigma_{vm}=\sqrt{a^{\star}(1-c^{\star})} (A.28)

This point is relevant to our drift results, where training under noisy conditions tends to converge toward this solution.

A.4.3 Exact gradient calculation

For the filter task considered here, the gradients with respect to the loss-visible overlaps (i.e., ∇σℒ\nabla_{\sigma}\mathcal{L}) can be derived in closed form.

Let e⁡(t)=y^​(t)−y⋆​(t)e(t)=\hat{y}(t)-y^{\star}(t) denote the output error. Writing the impulse-response coefficients as

A=σz​m−σz​u​σv​mσv​u,B=σz​u​σv​mσv​uA=\sigma_{zm}-\frac{\sigma_{zu}\sigma_{vm}}{\sigma_{vu}},\qquad B=\frac{\sigma_{zu}\sigma_{vm}}{\sigma_{vu}} (A.29)

the output takes the form

y^​(t)=A​e−t+B​e−(1−σv​u)​t\hat{y}(t)=A\,e^{-t}+B\,e^{-(1-\sigma_{vu})t} (A.30)

Define the difference

δ⁡(t)=e−(1−σv​u)​t−e−t\delta(t)=e^{-(1-\sigma_{vu})t}-e^{-t} (A.31)

The sensitivities of the output with respect to the loss-visible overlaps are

∂σz​my^​(t)\displaystyle\partial_{\sigma_{zm}}\hat{y}(t) =e−t\displaystyle=e^{-t} (A.32)
∂σz​uy^​(t)\displaystyle\partial_{\sigma_{zu}}\hat{y}(t) =σv​mσv​u​δ​(t)\displaystyle=\frac{\sigma_{vm}}{\sigma_{vu}}\,\delta(t)
∂σv​my^​(t)\displaystyle\partial_{\sigma_{vm}}\hat{y}(t) =σz​uσv​u​δ​(t)\displaystyle=\frac{\sigma_{zu}}{\sigma_{vu}}\,\delta(t)
∂σv​uy^​(t)\displaystyle\partial_{\sigma_{vu}}\hat{y}(t) =B⁡[−1σv​u​δ​(t)+t​e−(1−σv​u)​t]\displaystyle=B\!\left[-\frac{1}{\sigma_{vu}}\delta(t)+t\,e^{-(1-\sigma_{vu})t}\right]

For the episode loss ℒ=∫0T[y^​(t)−y⋆​(t)]2​𝑑t=∫0Te​(t)2​𝑑t\mathcal{L}=\int_{0}^{T}\bigl[\hat{y}(t)-y^{\star}(t)\bigr]^{2}\,dt=\int_{0}^{T}e(t)^{2}\,dt, the corresponding gradients are

∇z​m\displaystyle\nabla_{zm} =∂σz​mℒ=∫0Te⁡(t)​e−t​𝑑t\displaystyle=\partial_{\sigma_{zm}}\mathcal{L}=2\!\int_{0}^{T}e(t)\,e^{-t}\,dt (A.33)
∇z​u\displaystyle\nabla_{zu} =∂σz​uℒ=∫0Te⁡(t)​σv​mσv​u​δ​(t)​𝑑t\displaystyle=\partial_{\sigma_{zu}}\mathcal{L}=2\!\int_{0}^{T}e(t)\,\frac{\sigma_{vm}}{\sigma_{vu}}\delta(t)\,dt
∇v​m\displaystyle\nabla_{vm} =∂σv​mℒ=∫0Te⁡(t)​σz​uσv​u​δ​(t)​𝑑t\displaystyle=\partial_{\sigma_{vm}}\mathcal{L}=2\!\int_{0}^{T}e(t)\,\frac{\sigma_{zu}}{\sigma_{vu}}\delta(t)\,dt
∇v​u\displaystyle\nabla_{vu} =∂σv​uℒ=∫0Te⁡(t)​B​[−1σv​u​δ​(t)+t​e−(1−σv​u)​t]​𝑑t\displaystyle=\partial_{\sigma_{vu}}\mathcal{L}=2\!\int_{0}^{T}e(t)\,B\!\left[-\frac{1}{\sigma_{vu}}\delta(t)+t\,e^{-(1-\sigma_{vu})t}\right]dt

A.5 Differences between parameter-space and overlap-space learning

As noted in the main text, parameter-space gradient flow induces in overlap space the following dynamics 𝝈˙=−𝑮⁡(𝜽)​∇𝝈ℒ\dot{\bm{\sigma}}=-\bm{G}(\bm{\theta})\nabla_{\bm{\sigma}}\mathcal{L}, whereas direct overlap-space optimization follows 𝝈˙=−∇𝝈ℒ\dot{\bm{\sigma}}=-\nabla_{\bm{\sigma}}\mathcal{L}. The two dynamics follow the same path up to a rescaling of time whenever 𝑮⁡(𝜽)​∇𝝈ℒ=α⁡(t)​∇𝝈ℒ\bm{G}(\bm{\theta})\nabla_{\bm{\sigma}}\mathcal{L}=\alpha(t)\nabla_{\bm{\sigma}}\mathcal{L} for some α⁡(t)>0\alpha(t)>0, with 𝑮=α​𝑰\bm{G}=\alpha\bm{I} as a sufficient condition. More generally, however, anisotropic diagonal entries or off-diagonal mixing in 𝑮⁡(θ)\bm{G}(\theta) can alter the trajectory and the converged solution. To illustrate these possibilities, Fig. 6 compares parameter-induced and direct overlap-space learning dynamics on the linear filter task (see A.4) across three initialization regimes. For a balanced i.i.d. initialization, the metric is effectively isotropic, and the dynamics differ only by a time rescaling (blue). Introducing initial correlations through σm​u>0\sigma_{mu}>0 changes the trajectory but not the final solution (green), whereas an unbalanced initialization with ‖𝒖‖≫‖𝒗‖\|\bm{u}\|\gg\|\bm{v}\| changes both the trajectory and solution selected on the degenerate manifold (red).

A.6 An invariant under gradient flow

Define the N×2N\times 2 matrices

𝑨=[𝒛𝒗],𝑩=[𝒎𝒖]\bm{A}=\begin{bmatrix}\bm{z}&\bm{v}\end{bmatrix},\qquad\bm{B}=\begin{bmatrix}\bm{m}&\bm{u}\end{bmatrix} (A.34)

Note that 𝑨\bm{A} and 𝑩\bm{B} are disjoint, which will be important for the derivation below (and does not hold in the nonlinear case App. B). The four loss-visible overlaps assemble into the 2×22\times 2 matrix

1N​𝑨⊤​𝑩=1N​[𝒛⊤​𝒎𝒛⊤​𝒖𝒗⊤​𝒎𝒗⊤​𝒖]=[σz​mσz​uσv​mσv​u]\frac{1}{N}\bm{A}^{\top}\bm{B}=\frac{1}{N}\begin{bmatrix}\bm{z}^{\top}\bm{m}&\bm{z}^{\top}\bm{u}\\[2.0pt] \bm{v}^{\top}\bm{m}&\bm{v}^{\top}\bm{u}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\sigma_{zm}&\sigma_{zu}\\[2.0pt] \sigma_{vm}&\sigma_{vu}\end{bmatrix} (A.35)

Since the within-episode dynamics, readout, and loss depend on the parameters only through 1N​𝑨⊤​𝑩\tfrac{1}{N}\bm{A}^{\top}\bm{B}, the loss can be written as

ℒ=ℒ⁡(1N​𝑨⊤​𝑩)\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}(\tfrac{1}{N}\bm{A}^{\top}\bm{B}) (A.36)

Defining the 2×22\times 2 gradient matrix

𝑱=∂ℒ∂(𝑨⊤​𝑩)=[∇z​m∇z​u∇v​m∇v​u]\bm{J}=\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial(\bm{A}^{\top}\bm{B})}=\begin{bmatrix}\nabla_{zm}&\nabla_{zu}\\[2.0pt] \nabla_{vm}&\nabla_{vu}\end{bmatrix} (A.37)

gradient flow in parameter space takes the form

𝑨˙=−𝑩​𝑱⊤,𝑩˙=−𝑨​𝑱\dot{\bm{A}}=-\bm{B}\,\bm{J}^{\top},\qquad\dot{\bm{B}}=-\bm{A}\,\bm{J} (A.38)

which reproduces Eq. (A.10). Now, consider the matrix difference 𝑨​𝑨⊤−𝑩​𝑩⊤∈ℝN×N\bm{A}\bm{A}^{\top}-\bm{B}\bm{B}^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}

dd​τ​(𝑨​𝑨⊤)=−𝑩​𝑱⊤​𝑨⊤−𝑨​𝑱​𝑩⊤\frac{d}{d\tau}(\bm{A}\bm{A}^{\top})=-\bm{B}\bm{J}^{\top}\bm{A}^{\top}-\bm{A}\bm{J}\bm{B}^{\top} (A.39)

and similarly

dd​τ​(𝑩​𝑩⊤)=−𝑨​𝑱​𝑩⊤−𝑩​𝑱⊤​𝑨⊤\frac{d}{d\tau}(\bm{B}\bm{B}^{\top})=-\bm{A}\bm{J}\bm{B}^{\top}-\bm{B}\bm{J}^{\top}\bm{A}^{\top} (A.40)

Since the RHS of Eqs. (A.39), (A.40) are identical we have that

dd​τ​(𝑨​𝑨⊤−𝑩​𝑩⊤)=0\frac{d}{d\tau}\big(\bm{A}\bm{A}^{\top}-\bm{B}\bm{B}^{\top}\big)=0 (A.41)

Therefore the matrix

𝑲=𝑨​𝑨⊤−𝑩​𝑩⊤=𝒛​𝒛⊤+𝒗​𝒗⊤−𝒎​𝒎⊤−𝒖​𝒖⊤\bm{K}=\bm{A}\bm{A}^{\top}-\bm{B}\bm{B}^{\top}=\bm{z}\bm{z}^{\top}+\bm{v}\bm{v}^{\top}-\bm{m}\bm{m}^{\top}-\bm{u}\bm{u}^{\top} (A.42)

is conserved under gradient flow and is fixed entirely by the initialization (𝑨⁡(0),𝑩⁡(0))\big(\bm{A}(0),\bm{B}(0)\big).

Scalar Invariants

While 𝑲∈ℝN×N\bm{K}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N} is a high-dimensional matrix, it is constructed from only four vectors, implying rank⁡(𝑲)≤4\mathrm{rank}(\bm{K})\leq 4. Consequently, its conservation provides exactly four independent scalar constraints, given by the traces of its powers

𝒞k=Tr(𝑲k),k=1,…,4\mathcal{C}_{k}=\mathrm{Tr}(\bm{K}^{k}),\qquad k=1,\dots,4

Using the cyclic property of the trace, these invariants can be expressed directly in terms of the vector norms and pairwise overlaps. The first invariant (k=1k=1) is given by the squared norms of all connectivity vectors

𝒞1=Tr⁡(𝑲)=‖𝒛‖2+‖𝒗‖2−‖𝒎‖2−‖𝒖‖2\mathcal{C}_{1}=\mathrm{Tr}(\bm{K})=\|\bm{z}\|^{2}+\|\bm{v}\|^{2}-\|\bm{m}\|^{2}-\|\bm{u}\|^{2} (A.43)

The second invariant (k=2k=2) couples the norms and all overlaps

𝒞2=(‖𝒛‖4+‖𝒗‖4+2​σz​v2)+(‖𝒎‖4+‖𝒖‖4+2​σm​u2)−2​(σz​m2+σz​u2+σv​m2+σv​u2)\mathcal{C}_{2}=\left(\|\bm{z}\|^{4}+\|\bm{v}\|^{4}+2\sigma_{zv}^{2}\right)+\left(\|\bm{m}\|^{4}+\|\bm{u}\|^{4}+2\sigma_{mu}^{2}\right)-2\left(\sigma_{zm}^{2}+\sigma_{zu}^{2}+\sigma_{vm}^{2}+\sigma_{vu}^{2}\right) (A.44)

Similarly, 𝒞3\mathcal{C}_{3} and 𝒞4\mathcal{C}_{4} expand into increasingly complex overlap combinations. Collectively, these four scalar invariants constrain the 10-dimensional overlap system to a 6-dimensional manifold. From the gradient flow Eq. (A.14), the symmetry in the updates further implies that the differences ‖𝒛‖2−‖𝒎‖2\|\bm{z}\|^{2}-\|\bm{m}\|^{2} and ‖𝒗‖2−‖𝒖‖2\|\bm{v}\|^{2}-\|\bm{u}\|^{2} remain constant whenever σv​m​∇v​m=σz​u​∇z​u\sigma_{vm}\nabla_{vm}=\sigma_{zu}\nabla_{zu}, a condition satisfied for the filter task, due to the symmetric dependence of the loss on the product σz​u​σv​m\sigma_{zu}\sigma_{vm} (see Eq. (A.27)). Under these combined structural and task-specific constraints, there are insufficient degrees of freedom for the six loss-invisible overlaps to drift independently. Their evolution is thus tied to the initialization 𝑲\bm{K}, leading to an exact recovery observed in the A–B–A protocol.

Appendix B Nonlinear rank-1 RNN

We provide here a complete derivation of the learning dynamics of the nonlinear rank-1 RNN.

B.1 Within-episode dynamics

We consider a rank-1 recurrent network with nonlinear activation

𝒉˙​(t)=−𝒉⁡(t)+1N​𝒖​𝒗⊤​ϕ​(α​𝒉​(t))+𝒎​x​(t),ϕ⁡(x)=erf⁡(x),α=π/2\dot{\bm{h}}(t)=-\bm{h}(t)+\frac{1}{N}\bm{u}\bm{v}^{\top}\phi(\alpha\bm{h}(t))+\bm{m}\,x(t),\qquad\phi(x)=\mathrm{erf}(x),\qquad\alpha=\sqrt{\pi}/2 (B.1)

where the choice α=π/2\alpha=\sqrt{\pi}/2 ensures that the activation is locally linear with unit slope at the origin. As in the linear case, the recurrent term lies in span​{𝒖}\mathrm{span}\{\bm{u}\} and the input term lies in span​{𝒎}\mathrm{span}\{\bm{m}\}. Assuming 𝒉⁡(0)=𝟎\bm{h}(0)=\bm{0}, the state remains confined to

𝒉⁡(t)=κm​(t)​𝒎+κu​(t)​𝒖,𝜿⁡(t)=[κm​(t)κu​(t)]∈ℝ2\bm{h}(t)=\kappa_{m}(t)\bm{m}+\kappa_{u}(t)\bm{u},\qquad\bm{\kappa}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}\kappa_{m}(t)\\[2.0pt] \kappa_{u}(t)\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{2} (B.2)

Assuming that the parameter vectors have zero-mean, the activity also has zero mean, with empirical variance

Δ⁡(t)=1N​𝒉​(t)⊤​𝒉​(t)=κm2​‖𝒎‖2+κu2​‖𝒖‖2+2​κm​κu​σm​u\Delta(t)=\frac{1}{N}\bm{h}(t)^{\top}\bm{h}(t)=\kappa_{m}^{2}\|\bm{m}\|^{2}+\kappa_{u}^{2}\|\bm{u}\|^{2}+2\kappa_{m}\kappa_{u}\sigma_{mu} (B.3)

In the large-NN limit, neuron averages concentrate to expectations

1N​𝒗⊤​ϕ​(α​𝒉)=1N​∑ivi​ϕ​(α​hi)→N→∞𝔼⁡[vi​ϕ​(α​hi)]\frac{1}{N}\bm{v}^{\top}\phi(\alpha\bm{h})=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}v_{i}\phi(\alpha h_{i})\xrightarrow{N\to\infty}\mathbb{E}[v_{i}\phi(\alpha h_{i})] (B.4)

Following the dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) framework [27, 16], we assume that the components of the parameter vectors are jointly Gaussian. Since hi​(t)=κm​(t)​mi+κu​(t)​uih_{i}(t)=\kappa_{m}(t)m_{i}+\kappa_{u}(t)u_{i}, it follows that hi​(t)∼𝒩⁡(0,Δ⁡(t))h_{i}(t)\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Delta(t)). Applying Stein’s lemma to (vi,hi)(v_{i},h_{i}) gives

𝔼⁡[vi​ϕ​(α​hi)]=Cov⁡(vi,hi)​⟨ϕ′⟩\mathbb{E}[v_{i}\phi(\alpha h_{i})]=\operatorname{Cov}(v_{i},h_{i})\,\langle\phi^{\prime}\rangle (B.5)

where, for the error-function nonlinearity, that gain is given in closed-form

⟨ϕ′⟩=𝔼g∼𝒩⁡(0,Δ⁡(t))[αϕ′(αg)]=(1+π2Δ(t))−1/2\langle\phi^{\prime}\rangle=\mathbb{E}_{g\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Delta(t))}\left[\alpha\phi^{\prime}(\alpha g)\right]=\left(1+\frac{\pi}{2}\Delta(t)\right)^{-1/2} (B.6)

Using hi=κm​mi+κu​uih_{i}=\kappa_{m}m_{i}+\kappa_{u}u_{i} and the zero-mean assumption

Cov⁡(vi,hi)=κm​Cov⁡(vi,mi)+κu​Cov⁡(vi,ui)=σv​m​κm+σv​u​κu\operatorname{Cov}(v_{i},h_{i})=\kappa_{m}\operatorname{Cov}(v_{i},m_{i})+\kappa_{u}\operatorname{Cov}(v_{i},u_{i})=\sigma_{vm}\kappa_{m}+\sigma_{vu}\kappa_{u} (B.7)

Combining all together yields

1N​𝒗⊤​ϕ​(α​𝒉)=(σv​m​κm+σv​u​κu)​⟨ϕ′⟩\frac{1}{N}\bm{v}^{\top}\phi(\alpha\bm{h})=\left(\sigma_{vm}\kappa_{m}+\sigma_{vu}\kappa_{u}\right)\langle\phi^{\prime}\rangle (B.8)

Substituting into the dynamics, the NN-dimensional system reduces to

κ˙m​(t)\displaystyle\dot{\kappa}_{m}(t) =−κm​(t)+x⁡(t)\displaystyle=-\kappa_{m}(t)+x(t) (B.9)
κ˙u​(t)\displaystyle\dot{\kappa}_{u}(t) =−κu​(t)+(σv​m​κm​(t)+σv​u​κu​(t))​⟨ϕ′⟩\displaystyle=-\kappa_{u}(t)+\left(\sigma_{vm}\kappa_{m}(t)+\sigma_{vu}\kappa_{u}(t)\right)\langle\phi^{\prime}\rangle

Applying the same argument to (zi,hi)(z_{i},h_{i}) gives

y^​(t)=(σz​m​κm​(t)+σz​u​κu​(t))​⟨ϕ′⟩\hat{y}(t)=\left(\sigma_{zm}\kappa_{m}(t)+\sigma_{zu}\kappa_{u}(t)\right)\langle\phi^{\prime}\rangle (B.10)

Note that, unlike in the linear case, the variance Δ⁡(t)\Delta(t) depends on the overlap σm​u\sigma_{mu} as well as the norms ‖𝒎‖2\|\bm{m}\|^{2} and ‖𝒖‖2\|\bm{u}\|^{2}. As a result, these quantities directly influence the network dynamics and output, and therefore become loss-visible.

B.2 Across-episode learning dynamics

The episode loss depends on the parameters only through the new set of loss-visible overlaps

ℒ=ℒ⁡(σz​m,σz​u,σv​m,σv​u,σm​u,‖𝒎‖2,‖𝒖‖2)\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}\bigl(\sigma_{zm},\sigma_{zu},\sigma_{vm},\sigma_{vu},\sigma_{mu},\|\bm{m}\|^{2},\|\bm{u}\|^{2}\bigr) (B.11)

Using ∇m​m=∂ℒ/∂‖𝒎‖2\nabla_{mm}=\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial\|\bm{m}\|^{2} and ∇u​u=∂ℒ/∂‖𝒖‖2\nabla_{uu}=\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial\|\bm{u}\|^{2}, together with ∂‖𝒎‖2/∂𝒎=2​𝒎/N\partial\|\bm{m}\|^{2}/\partial\bm{m}=2\bm{m}/N and ∂‖𝒖‖2/∂𝒖=2​𝒖/N\partial\|\bm{u}\|^{2}/\partial\bm{u}=2\bm{u}/N, the chain rule gives

∂ℒ∂𝒎\displaystyle\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\bm{m}} =1N​(∇z​m𝒛+∇v​m𝒗+∇m​u𝒖+2​∇m​m𝒎)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}(\nabla_{zm}\,\bm{z}+\nabla_{vm}\,\bm{v}+\nabla_{mu}\,\bm{u}+2\nabla_{mm}\,\bm{m}) (B.12)
∂ℒ∂𝒖\displaystyle\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\bm{u}} =1N​(∇z​u𝒛+∇v​u𝒗+∇m​u𝒎+2​∇u​u𝒖)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}(\nabla_{zu}\,\bm{z}+\nabla_{vu}\,\bm{v}+\nabla_{mu}\,\bm{m}+2\nabla_{uu}\,\bm{u}) (B.13)
∂ℒ∂𝒛\displaystyle\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\bm{z}} =1N​(∇z​m𝒎+∇z​u𝒖)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}(\nabla_{zm}\,\bm{m}+\nabla_{zu}\,\bm{u}) (B.14)
∂ℒ∂𝒗\displaystyle\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\bm{v}} =1N​(∇v​m𝒎+∇v​u𝒖)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}(\nabla_{vm}\,\bm{m}+\nabla_{vu}\,\bm{u})

Under gradient flow 𝜽˙=−∇𝜽ℒ\dot{\bm{\theta}}=-\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}\mathcal{L} we obtain

𝒎˙\displaystyle\dot{\bm{m}} =−1N​(∇z​m𝒛+∇v​m𝒗+∇m​u𝒖+2​∇m​m𝒎)\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{N}(\nabla_{zm}\bm{z}+\nabla_{vm}\bm{v}+\nabla_{mu}\bm{u}+2\nabla_{mm}\bm{m}) (B.15)
𝒖˙\displaystyle\dot{\bm{u}} =−1N​(∇z​u𝒛+∇v​u𝒗+∇m​u𝒎+2​∇u​u𝒖)\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{N}(\nabla_{zu}\bm{z}+\nabla_{vu}\bm{v}+\nabla_{mu}\bm{m}+2\nabla_{uu}\bm{u})
𝒗˙\displaystyle\dot{\bm{v}} =−1N​(∇v​m𝒎+∇v​u𝒖)\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{N}(\nabla_{vm}\bm{m}+\nabla_{vu}\bm{u})
𝒛˙\displaystyle\dot{\bm{z}} =−1N​(∇z​m𝒎+∇z​u𝒖)\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{N}(\nabla_{zm}\bm{m}+\nabla_{zu}\bm{u})

By the product rule of the overlaps, we obtain the dynamics for the loss-visible overlaps

σ˙z​m\displaystyle\dot{\sigma}_{zm} =−(‖𝒎‖2+‖𝒛‖2)​∇z​m−σm​u​∇z​u−σz​v​∇v​m−σz​u​∇m​u−2​∇m​mσz​m\displaystyle=-(\|\bm{m}\|^{2}+\|\bm{z}\|^{2})\nabla_{zm}-\sigma_{mu}\nabla_{zu}-\sigma_{zv}\nabla_{vm}-\sigma_{zu}\nabla_{mu}-2\nabla_{mm}\sigma_{zm} (B.16)
σ˙z​u\displaystyle\dot{\sigma}_{zu} =−σm​u​∇z​m−(‖𝒖‖2+‖𝒛‖2)​∇z​u−σz​v​∇v​u−σz​m​∇m​u−2​∇u​uσz​u\displaystyle=-\sigma_{mu}\nabla_{zm}-(\|\bm{u}\|^{2}+\|\bm{z}\|^{2})\nabla_{zu}-\sigma_{zv}\nabla_{vu}-\sigma_{zm}\nabla_{mu}-2\nabla_{uu}\sigma_{zu}
σ˙v​m\displaystyle\dot{\sigma}_{vm} =−(‖𝒎‖2+‖𝒗‖2)​∇v​m−σm​u​∇v​u−σz​v​∇z​m−σv​u​∇m​u−2​∇m​mσv​m\displaystyle=-(\|\bm{m}\|^{2}+\|\bm{v}\|^{2})\nabla_{vm}-\sigma_{mu}\nabla_{vu}-\sigma_{zv}\nabla_{zm}-\sigma_{vu}\nabla_{mu}-2\nabla_{mm}\sigma_{vm}
σ˙v​u\displaystyle\dot{\sigma}_{vu} =−σm​u​∇v​m−(‖𝒖‖2+‖𝒗‖2)​∇v​u−σz​v​∇z​u−σv​m​∇m​u−2​∇u​uσv​u\displaystyle=-\sigma_{mu}\nabla_{vm}-(\|\bm{u}\|^{2}+\|\bm{v}\|^{2})\nabla_{vu}-\sigma_{zv}\nabla_{zu}-\sigma_{vm}\nabla_{mu}-2\nabla_{uu}\sigma_{vu}
σ˙m​u\displaystyle\dot{\sigma}_{mu} =−σz​u​∇z​m−σz​m​∇z​u−σv​u​∇v​m−σv​m​∇v​u−(‖𝒎‖2+‖𝒖‖2)​∇m​u−2​(∇m​m+∇u​u)​σm​u\displaystyle=-\sigma_{zu}\nabla_{zm}-\sigma_{zm}\nabla_{zu}-\sigma_{vu}\nabla_{vm}-\sigma_{vm}\nabla_{vu}-(\|\bm{m}\|^{2}+\|\bm{u}\|^{2})\nabla_{mu}-2(\nabla_{mm}+\nabla_{uu})\sigma_{mu}
‖𝒎‖2˙\displaystyle\dot{\|\bm{m}\|^{2}} =−2​(σz​m​∇z​m+σv​m​∇v​m+σm​u​∇m​u+2​∇m​m‖𝒎‖2)\displaystyle=-2\Bigl(\sigma_{zm}\nabla_{zm}+\sigma_{vm}\nabla_{vm}+\sigma_{mu}\nabla_{mu}+2\nabla_{mm}\|\bm{m}\|^{2}\Bigr)
‖𝒖‖2˙\displaystyle\dot{\|\bm{u}\|^{2}} =−2​(σz​u​∇z​u+σv​u​∇v​u+σm​u​∇m​u+2​∇u​u‖𝒖‖2)\displaystyle=-2\Bigl(\sigma_{zu}\nabla_{zu}+\sigma_{vu}\nabla_{vu}+\sigma_{mu}\nabla_{mu}+2\nabla_{uu}\|\bm{u}\|^{2}\Bigr)

as well as the loss-invisible dynamics

σ˙z​v\displaystyle\dot{\sigma}_{zv} =−σv​m​∇z​m−σv​u​∇z​u−σz​m​∇v​m−σz​u​∇v​u\displaystyle=-\sigma_{vm}\nabla_{zm}-\sigma_{vu}\nabla_{zu}-\sigma_{zm}\nabla_{vm}-\sigma_{zu}\nabla_{vu} (B.17)
‖𝒗‖2˙\displaystyle\dot{\|\bm{v}\|^{2}} =−2​(σv​m​∇v​m+σv​u​∇v​u)\displaystyle=-2\Bigl(\sigma_{vm}\nabla_{vm}+\sigma_{vu}\nabla_{vu}\Bigr)
‖𝒛‖2˙\displaystyle\dot{\|\bm{z}\|^{2}} =−2​(σz​m​∇z​m+σz​u​∇z​u)\displaystyle=-2\Bigl(\sigma_{zm}\nabla_{zm}+\sigma_{zu}\nabla_{zu}\Bigr)

B.3 Learning dynamics in matrix form

Define

𝝈=[σz​mσz​uσv​mσv​uσm​u‖𝒎‖2‖𝒖‖2],𝝈~=[σz​v‖𝒗‖2‖𝒛‖2],∇𝝈ℒ=∂ℒ∂𝝈=[∇z​m∇z​u∇v​m∇v​u∇m​u∇‖𝒎‖2∇‖𝒖‖2]\bm{\sigma}=\begin{bmatrix}\sigma_{zm}\\ \sigma_{zu}\\ \sigma_{vm}\\ \sigma_{vu}\\ \sigma_{mu}\\ \|\bm{m}\|^{2}\\ \|\bm{u}\|^{2}\end{bmatrix},\qquad\tilde{\bm{\sigma}}=\begin{bmatrix}\sigma_{zv}\\ \|\bm{v}\|^{2}\\ \|\bm{z}\|^{2}\end{bmatrix},\qquad\nabla_{\bm{\sigma}}\mathcal{L}=\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\bm{\sigma}}=\begin{bmatrix}\nabla_{zm}\\ \nabla_{zu}\\ \nabla_{vm}\\ \nabla_{vu}\\ \nabla_{mu}\\ \nabla_{\|\bm{m}\|^{2}}\\ \nabla_{\|\bm{u}\|^{2}}\end{bmatrix} (B.18)

The loss-visible Gram matrix 𝑮∈ℝ7×7\bm{G}\in\mathbb{R}^{7\times 7} is

𝑮⁡(𝜽)=1N​[‖𝒎‖2+‖𝒛‖2σm​uσz​v0σz​u2​σz​m0σm​u‖𝒖‖2+‖𝒛‖20σz​vσz​m02​σz​uσz​v0‖𝒎‖2+‖𝒗‖2σm​uσv​u2​σv​m00σz​vσm​u‖𝒖‖2+‖𝒗‖2σv​m02​σv​uσz​uσz​mσv​uσv​m‖𝒎‖2+‖𝒖‖22​σm​u2​σm​u2​σz​m02​σv​m02​σm​u4​‖𝒎‖2002​σz​u02​σv​u2​σm​u04​‖𝒖‖2]\displaystyle\bm{G}(\bm{\theta})=\frac{1}{N}\begin{bmatrix}\|\bm{m}\|^{2}+\|\bm{z}\|^{2}&\sigma_{mu}&\sigma_{zv}&0&\sigma_{zu}&2\sigma_{zm}&0\\ \sigma_{mu}&\|\bm{u}\|^{2}+\|\bm{z}\|^{2}&0&\sigma_{zv}&\sigma_{zm}&0&2\sigma_{zu}\\ \sigma_{zv}&0&\|\bm{m}\|^{2}+\|\bm{v}\|^{2}&\sigma_{mu}&\sigma_{vu}&2\sigma_{vm}&0\\ 0&\sigma_{zv}&\sigma_{mu}&\|\bm{u}\|^{2}+\|\bm{v}\|^{2}&\sigma_{vm}&0&2\sigma_{vu}\\ \sigma_{zu}&\sigma_{zm}&\sigma_{vu}&\sigma_{vm}&\|\bm{m}\|^{2}+\|\bm{u}\|^{2}&2\sigma_{mu}&2\sigma_{mu}\\ 2\sigma_{zm}&0&2\sigma_{vm}&0&2\sigma_{mu}&4\|\bm{m}\|^{2}&0\\ 0&2\sigma_{zu}&0&2\sigma_{vu}&2\sigma_{mu}&0&4\|\bm{u}\|^{2}\end{bmatrix} (B.19)

and the loss-invisible matrix 𝑮~∈ℝ3×7\tilde{\bm{G}}\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times 7} is

𝑮~​(𝜽)=1N​[σv​mσv​uσz​mσz​u000002​σv​m2​σv​u0002​σz​m2​σz​u00000]\tilde{\bm{G}}(\bm{\theta})=\frac{1}{N}\begin{bmatrix}\sigma_{vm}&\sigma_{vu}&\sigma_{zm}&\sigma_{zu}&0&0&0\\ 0&0&2\sigma_{vm}&2\sigma_{vu}&0&0&0\\ 2\sigma_{zm}&2\sigma_{zu}&0&0&0&0&0\end{bmatrix} (B.20)

Using these definitions, the learning dynamics can be written compactly as

𝝈˙=−𝑮⁡(𝜽)​∇𝝈ℒ,𝝈~˙=−𝑮~​(𝜽)​∇𝝈ℒ\dot{\bm{\sigma}}=-\bm{G}(\bm{\theta})\,\nabla_{\bm{\sigma}}\mathcal{L},\qquad\dot{\tilde{\bm{\sigma}}}=-\tilde{\bm{G}}(\bm{\theta})\,\nabla_{\bm{\sigma}}\mathcal{L} (B.21)

B.4 Flip-flop task

For our nonlinear presentation, we consider the 1-bit flip-flop task [36] (Fig. 10d). The task requires the network to act as a bistable memory: it must maintain a constant output and only "flip" its state upon receiving a brief, signed input pulse. This behavior requires the creation of stable fixed points separated by a nonlinear boundary. During each trial, the network receives a sequence of short input pulses, each of duration tstimt_{\mathrm{stim}}. During a pulse, the input channel is set to x⁡(t)=s​xampx(t)=s\,x_{\mathrm{amp}}, where xamp=1x_{\mathrm{amp}}=1, and the sign s∈{±1}s\in\{\pm 1\} is chosen at random. Each pulse is followed by a delay period of duration tdelayt_{\mathrm{delay}}, after which a decision period begins. During this decision period, the loss is activated (i.e., a mask is set to 1), and the target value is defined as y⁡(t)=s​yamp{y}(t)=s\,{y}_{\mathrm{amp}}, with yamp=0.5y_{\mathrm{amp}}=0.5. The decision period ends when the next pulse begins. The inter-stimulus delays tisdt_{\mathrm{isd}} are drawn randomly.

B.4.1 Training details, RNN initialization and Gaussian assumption

Numerical simulations were performed by training a continuous-time rank-1 RNN discretized Euler method with time step Δ​t=0.025\Delta t=0.025 and network size N=1000N=1000. Every element of the trainable vectors 𝜽={𝒎,𝒖,𝒗,𝒛}⊂ℝN\bm{\theta}=\{\bm{m},\bm{u},\bm{v},\bm{z}\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{N} is initialized i.i.d. from a standard normal distribution 𝒩⁡(0,1)\mathcal{N}(0,1). Training is performed using gradient descent with learning rate η=0.05\eta=0.05 over episodes of length T=20​sT=20\,\mathrm{s} and batch size of 10. We use a masked mean-squared error (MSE) loss that ignores the output during input pulses and short transients, thereby focusing learning on maintaining stable fixed-point outputs.

Furthermore, unlike the linear case, the nonlinear theory relies on the components of the high-dimensional parameter vectors 𝜽\bm{\theta} remaining approximately Gaussian during training. Here, we complement the main text by (i) verifying that the weights remain approximately Gaussian under a small learning rate (η=0.05\eta=0.05; Fig. 9a), and (ii) showing that when this assumption breaks (e.g., with larger learning rates (η=0.5\eta=0.5) or Adam (η=0.001\eta=0.001)), the theory is no longer valid (Fig 9b,c).

B.5 History-dependent training protocol

We consider a history-dependent training protocol consisting of three tasks. Task A is identical to the flip-flop task described above (B.4). Task B is a stimulus-integration decision-making task (see below). And Task C is a teacher-student task, where both networks are trained to reproduce the output of a pre-defined teacher network in response to white noise input (Fig. 10f). The teacher network overlaps are defined as

(σz​m,σz​u,σv​m,σv​u,σm​u,∥𝒎∥2,∥𝒖∥2)=(0.5, 2.3, 2.0, 1.5, 1.6, 1.8, 2.2)\bigl(\sigma_{zm},\sigma_{zu},\sigma_{vm},\sigma_{vu},\sigma_{mu},\|\bm{m}\|^{2},\|\bm{u}\|^{2}\bigl)=\bigl(0.5,\,2.3,\,2.0,\,1.5,\,1.6,\,1.8,\,2.2\bigl)

Training proceeds in two phases: Phase A/B and Phase C. In Phase A/B, networks are trained on either Task A or Task B for 30,000 epochs, using an initial learning rate of η=0.01\eta=0.01. The learning rate is reduced by a factor of 5 whenever the loss falls below 0.0150.015. In Phase C, training continues for an additional 30,000 epochs with a fixed learning rate of η=0.001\eta=0.001. To ensure consistency with the Gaussian assumptions underlying the low-dimensional nonlinear theory, training is performed directly in the overlap space using the corresponding preconditioned 𝑮\bm{G}. The initial overlap values are sampled as follows: cross-overlaps σz​m,σz​u,σv​m,σv​u,σm​u,σz​v\sigma_{zm},\sigma_{zu},\sigma_{vm},\sigma_{vu},\sigma_{mu},\sigma_{zv} are drawn from |𝒩⁡(0,0.4)||\mathcal{N}(0,0.4)|, and the squared norms ‖𝒎‖2,‖𝒖‖2,‖𝒗‖2,‖𝒛‖2\|\bm{m}\|^{2},\|\bm{u}\|^{2},\|\bm{v}\|^{2},\|\bm{z}\|^{2} are drawn uniformly from 𝒰⁡[0.5,2.0]\mathcal{U}[0.5,2.0]. Within-episode dynamics are integrated with time step Δ​t=0.05\Delta t=0.05 over episodes of length T=20​sT=20\,\mathrm{s}. For both phases, we used a batch size of 128.

Decision-making task

This task requires the network to integrate a noisy evidence input to produce a continuous output proportional to the stimulus strength (Fig. 10e). Each trial consists of a stimulus period of duration tstimt_{\mathrm{stim}}, a brief delay tdelayt_{\mathrm{delay}}, and a response period. During the stimulus period, the input channel receives a noisy signal x⁡(t)=c+ξ⁡(t)x(t)=c+\xi(t), where cc is a coherence level chosen from a discrete set 𝒞∈{±2,±8,±16}\mathcal{C}\in\{\pm 2,\pm 8,\pm 16\} and ξ⁡(t)∼𝒩⁡(0,0.052)\xi(t)\sim\mathcal{N}(0,0.05^{2}) is zero-mean Gaussian noise. During the response period the target value is defined as y⁡(t)=yamp​(c/cmax)y(t)=y_{\mathrm{amp}}(c/c_{\mathrm{max}}), with yamp=1.0y_{\mathrm{amp}}=1.0 and cmaxc_{\mathrm{max}} is the maximum absolute coherence. The network is trained using a masked mean squared error (MSE) loss that is active only during the decision period.

Classification

To test whether task history can be decoded from the overlaps, we trained a logistic-regression classifier (the precise choice of classifier is not critical; similar results are obtained using SVM) to classify networks first trained on Task A from those first trained on Task B. Overlap vectors were extracted from 10 independent runs (10 ×\times 2 twins network) at three stages: initialization, after Phase A/B, and after Phase C. Classification was performed separately using either the loss-visible or loss-invisible overlaps. At each stage, the 20 samples (10 per class) were split into training and test sets (16/4), and evaluation was repeated over 50 random splits. Performance is reported as the mean and standard deviation of test accuracy across splits. Importantly, before classification, white noise was added to the overlap features to both reflect realistic variability and prevent the classifier from exploiting infinitesimal differences arising from imperfect convergence (see Fig. 11; the results are largely insensitive to the precise choice of noise level).

Appendix C Derivation of the augmented Gram matrix 𝑮¯\bar{\bm{G}}

To derive the augmented 𝑮¯\bar{\bm{G}} matrix, we define 𝝈¯​(𝜽)\bar{\bm{\sigma}}(\bm{\theta}) as the exhaustive collection of all quadratic scalars formable from the four vectors {𝒎,𝒖,𝒗,𝒛}\{\bm{m},\bm{u},\bm{v},\bm{z}\}. This set comprises the six pairwise overlaps and the four squared norms, encompassing both loss-visible and loss-invisible quantities

𝜽=[𝒎𝒖𝒗𝒛]∈ℝ4​N,𝝈¯​(𝜽)=[σz​mσz​uσv​mσv​uσm​uσz​v‖𝒎‖2‖𝒖‖2‖𝒗‖2‖𝒛‖2]∈ℝ10\bm{\theta}=\begin{bmatrix}\bm{m}\\ \bm{u}\\ \bm{v}\\ \bm{z}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{4N},\qquad\bar{\bm{\sigma}}(\bm{\theta})=\begin{bmatrix}\sigma_{zm}\\ \sigma_{zu}\\ \sigma_{vm}\\ \sigma_{vu}\\ \sigma_{mu}\\ \sigma_{zv}\\ \|\bm{m}\|^{2}\\ \|\bm{u}\|^{2}\\ \|\bm{v}\|^{2}\\ \|\bm{z}\|^{2}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{10} (C.1)

The full Jacobian is given by

𝑫¯​(𝜽)=∂𝝈¯∂𝜽=1N​[𝒛⊤00𝒎⊤0𝒛⊤0𝒖⊤𝒗⊤0𝒎⊤00𝒗⊤𝒖⊤0𝒖⊤𝒎⊤0000𝒛⊤𝒗⊤2​𝒎⊤00002​𝒖⊤00002​𝒗⊤00002​𝒛⊤]∈ℝ10×4​N\bar{\bm{D}}(\bm{\theta})=\frac{\partial\bar{\bm{\sigma}}}{\partial\bm{\theta}}\;=\;\frac{1}{N}\begin{bmatrix}\bm{z}^{\top}&0&0&\bm{m}^{\top}\\ 0&\bm{z}^{\top}&0&\bm{u}^{\top}\\ \bm{v}^{\top}&0&\bm{m}^{\top}&0\\ 0&\bm{v}^{\top}&\bm{u}^{\top}&0\\ \bm{u}^{\top}&\bm{m}^{\top}&0&0\\ 0&0&\bm{z}^{\top}&\bm{v}^{\top}\\ 2\bm{m}^{\top}&0&0&0\\ 0&2\bm{u}^{\top}&0&0\\ 0&0&2\bm{v}^{\top}&0\\ 0&0&0&2\bm{z}^{\top}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{10\times 4N} (C.2)

and the associated 10×1010\times 10 Gram matrix, defined as 𝑮¯​(𝜽)=𝑫¯​(𝜽)​𝑫¯​(𝜽)⊤\bar{\bm{G}}(\bm{\theta})=\bar{\bm{D}}(\bm{\theta})\bar{\bm{D}}(\bm{\theta})^{\top}

1N​[‖𝒛‖2+‖𝒎‖2σm​uσz​v0σz​uσv​m2​σz​m002​σz​mσm​u‖𝒛‖2+‖𝒖‖20σz​vσz​mσv​u02​σz​u02​σz​uσz​v0‖𝒗‖2+‖𝒎‖2σm​uσv​uσz​m2​σv​m02​σv​m00σz​vσm​u‖𝒗‖2+‖𝒖‖2σv​mσz​u02​σv​u2​σv​u0σz​uσz​mσv​uσv​m‖𝒎‖2+‖𝒖‖202​σm​u2​σm​u00σv​mσv​uσz​mσz​u0‖𝒛‖2+‖𝒗‖2002​σz​v2​σz​v2​σz​m02​σv​m02​σm​u04​‖𝒎‖200002​σz​u02​σv​u2​σm​u004​‖𝒖‖200002​σv​m2​σv​u02​σz​v004​‖𝒗‖202​σz​m2​σz​u0002​σz​v0004​‖𝒛‖2]{\normalsize\frac{1}{N}\begin{bmatrix}\|\bm{z}\|^{2}+\|\bm{m}\|^{2}&\sigma_{mu}&\sigma_{zv}&0&\sigma_{zu}&\sigma_{vm}&2\sigma_{zm}&0&0&2\sigma_{zm}\\ \sigma_{mu}&\|\bm{z}\|^{2}+\|\bm{u}\|^{2}&0&\sigma_{zv}&\sigma_{zm}&\sigma_{vu}&0&2\sigma_{zu}&0&2\sigma_{zu}\\ \sigma_{zv}&0&\|\bm{v}\|^{2}+\|\bm{m}\|^{2}&\sigma_{mu}&\sigma_{vu}&\sigma_{zm}&2\sigma_{vm}&0&2\sigma_{vm}&0\\ 0&\sigma_{zv}&\sigma_{mu}&\|\bm{v}\|^{2}+\|\bm{u}\|^{2}&\sigma_{vm}&\sigma_{zu}&0&2\sigma_{vu}&2\sigma_{vu}&0\\ \sigma_{zu}&\sigma_{zm}&\sigma_{vu}&\sigma_{vm}&\|\bm{m}\|^{2}+\|\bm{u}\|^{2}&0&2\sigma_{mu}&2\sigma_{mu}&0&0\\ \sigma_{vm}&\sigma_{vu}&\sigma_{zm}&\sigma_{zu}&0&\|\bm{z}\|^{2}+\|\bm{v}\|^{2}&0&0&2\sigma_{zv}&2\sigma_{zv}\\ 2\sigma_{zm}&0&2\sigma_{vm}&0&2\sigma_{mu}&0&4\|\bm{m}\|^{2}&0&0&0\\ 0&2\sigma_{zu}&0&2\sigma_{vu}&2\sigma_{mu}&0&0&4\|\bm{u}\|^{2}&0&0\\ 0&0&2\sigma_{vm}&2\sigma_{vu}&0&2\sigma_{zv}&0&0&4\|\bm{v}\|^{2}&0\\ 2\sigma_{zm}&2\sigma_{zu}&0&0&0&2\sigma_{zv}&0&0&0&4\|\bm{z}\|^{2}\end{bmatrix}} (C.3)

Crucially, these derivations hold for any RNN where the connectivity is formed by these four vectors. While the network’s nonlinearity changes the functional form of the loss, it does not change the Jacobian 𝑫¯\bar{\bm{D}} or the Gram matrix 𝑮¯\bar{\bm{G}}. The network linearity simply sets the boundary between visible and invisible overlaps, shaping how gradient flow evolves in overlap space (Fig. 12).

Appendix D Rank-2 linear RNN

We provide a brief extension of our analysis to a rank-2 linear RNN with recurrent connectivity

𝑾=1N​∑j=12𝒖j​𝒗j⊤\bm{W}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{2}\bm{u}_{j}\bm{v}_{j}^{\top} (D.1)

The parameter set consists of six vectors {𝒎,𝒖1,𝒖2,𝒗2,𝒗2,𝒛}⊂ℝN\{\bm{m},\bm{u}_{1},\bm{u}_{2},\bm{v}_{2},\bm{v}_{2},\bm{z}\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{N}. With zero initial condition 𝒉⁡(0)=𝟎\bm{h}(0)=\bm{0}, the dynamics remain confined to the 3-dimensional subspace span⁡{𝒎,𝒖1,𝒖2}\mathrm{span}\{\bm{m},\bm{u}_{1},\bm{u}_{2}\}. We write

𝒉⁡(t)=κm​(t)​𝒎+κu1​(t)​𝒖1+κu2​(t)​𝒖2,𝜿⁡(t)=[κmκu1κu2]\bm{h}(t)=\kappa_{m}(t)\bm{m}+\kappa_{u_{1}}(t)\bm{u}_{1}+\kappa_{u_{2}}(t)\bm{u}_{2},\qquad\bm{\kappa}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}\kappa_{m}\\ \kappa_{u_{1}}\\ \kappa_{u_{2}}\end{bmatrix} (D.2)

The effective within-episode dynamics and readout are

𝜿˙​(t)\displaystyle\dot{\bm{\kappa}}(t) =−𝜿⁡(t)+[000σv1​mσv1​u1σv1​u2σv2​mσv2​u1σv2​u2]​𝜿​(t)+[100]​x​(t)\displaystyle=-\bm{\kappa}(t)+\begin{bmatrix}0&0&0\\ \sigma_{v_{1}m}&\sigma_{v_{1}u_{1}}&\sigma_{v_{1}u_{2}}\\ \sigma_{v_{2}m}&\sigma_{v_{2}u_{1}}&\sigma_{v_{2}u_{2}}\end{bmatrix}\bm{\kappa}(t)+\begin{bmatrix}1\\ 0\\ 0\end{bmatrix}x(t) (D.3)
y^​(t)\displaystyle\hat{y}(t) =[σz​mσz​u1σz​u2]​𝜿​(t)\displaystyle=\begin{bmatrix}\sigma_{zm}&\sigma_{zu_{1}}&\sigma_{zu_{2}}\end{bmatrix}\bm{\kappa}(t)

Thus, the input–output map, and hence the loss, is fully determined by 9 loss-visible overlaps. To derive the resulting overlap dynamics, we introduce a compact matrix formulation (alternative to that presented in the main text) that scales naturally to higher-rank networks. To this end, we collect the six parameter vectors into

𝚯=[𝒎𝒖1𝒖2𝒗1𝒗2𝒛]∈ℝN×6\bm{\Theta}=\begin{bmatrix}\bm{m}&\bm{u}_{1}&\bm{u}_{2}&\bm{v}_{1}&\bm{v}_{2}&\bm{z}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times 6} (D.4)

and define the Gram matrix 𝑸\bm{Q}, which contains all 21 pairwise overlaps

𝑸=1N​𝚯⊤​𝚯=[‖𝒎‖2σm​u1σm​u2σv1​mσv2​mσz​mσm​u1‖𝒖1‖2σu1​u2σv1​u1σv2​u1σz​u1σm​u2σu1​u2‖𝒖2‖2σv1​u2σv2​u2σz​u2σv1​mσv1​u1σv1​u2‖𝒗1‖2σv1​v2σz​v1σv2​mσv2​u1σv2​u2σv1​v2‖𝒗2‖2σz​v2σz​mσz​u1σz​u2σz​v1σz​v2‖𝒛‖2]\bm{Q}=\frac{1}{N}\bm{\Theta}^{\top}\bm{\Theta}=\begin{bmatrix}\|\bm{m}\|^{2}&\sigma_{mu_{1}}&\sigma_{mu_{2}}&\sigma_{v_{1}m}&\sigma_{v_{2}m}&\sigma_{zm}\\ \sigma_{mu_{1}}&\|\bm{u}_{1}\|^{2}&\sigma_{u_{1}u_{2}}&\sigma_{v_{1}u_{1}}&\sigma_{v_{2}u_{1}}&\sigma_{zu_{1}}\\ \sigma_{mu_{2}}&\sigma_{u_{1}u_{2}}&\|\bm{u}_{2}\|^{2}&\sigma_{v_{1}u_{2}}&\sigma_{v_{2}u_{2}}&\sigma_{zu_{2}}\\ \sigma_{v_{1}m}&\sigma_{v_{1}u_{1}}&\sigma_{v_{1}u_{2}}&\|\bm{v}_{1}\|^{2}&\sigma_{v_{1}v_{2}}&\sigma_{zv_{1}}\\ \sigma_{v_{2}m}&\sigma_{v_{2}u_{1}}&\sigma_{v_{2}u_{2}}&\sigma_{v_{1}v_{2}}&\|\bm{v}_{2}\|^{2}&\sigma_{zv_{2}}\\ \sigma_{zm}&\sigma_{zu_{1}}&\sigma_{zu_{2}}&\sigma_{zv_{1}}&\sigma_{zv_{2}}&\|\bm{z}\|^{2}\end{bmatrix} (D.5)

Note that 𝑸\bm{Q} is distinct from the preconditioning Gram matrix 𝑮=𝑫​𝑫⊤\bm{G}=\bm{D}\bm{D}^{\top} introduced in the main text. The nine cross-block entries of 𝑸\bm{Q} are loss-visible, whereas the remaining 12 entries are loss-invisible. Let ∇a​b=∂ℒ/∂σa​b\nabla_{ab}=\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial\sigma_{ab}, and define the symmetric gradient matrix

𝑴=[000∇v1​m∇v2​m∇z​m000∇v1​u1∇v2​u1∇z​u1000∇v1​u2∇v2​u2∇z​u2∇v1​m∇v1​u1∇v1​u2000∇v2​m∇v2​u1∇v2​u2000∇z​m∇z​u1∇z​u2000]\bm{M}=\begin{bmatrix}0&0&0&\nabla_{v_{1}m}&\nabla_{v_{2}m}&\nabla_{zm}\\ 0&0&0&\nabla_{v_{1}u_{1}}&\nabla_{v_{2}u_{1}}&\nabla_{zu_{1}}\\ 0&0&0&\nabla_{v_{1}u_{2}}&\nabla_{v_{2}u_{2}}&\nabla_{zu_{2}}\\ \nabla_{v_{1}m}&\nabla_{v_{1}u_{1}}&\nabla_{v_{1}u_{2}}&0&0&0\\ \nabla_{v_{2}m}&\nabla_{v_{2}u_{1}}&\nabla_{v_{2}u_{2}}&0&0&0\\ \nabla_{zm}&\nabla_{zu_{1}}&\nabla_{zu_{2}}&0&0&0\end{bmatrix} (D.6)

Because the loss depends only on the visible overlaps, gradient flow in parameter space is given by

𝚯˙=−1N​𝚯​𝑴\dot{\bm{\Theta}}=-\frac{1}{N}\bm{\Theta}\bm{M} (D.7)

Using 𝑸=𝚯⊤​𝚯/N\bm{Q}=\bm{\Theta}^{\top}\bm{\Theta}/N and the product rule, we obtain

𝑸˙=1N​(𝚯˙⊤​𝚯+𝚯⊤​𝚯˙)=−1N​(𝑴​𝑸+𝑸​𝑴)\dot{\bm{Q}}=\frac{1}{N}\left(\dot{\bm{\Theta}}^{\top}\bm{\Theta}+\bm{\Theta}^{\top}\dot{\bm{\Theta}}\right)=-\frac{1}{N}\left(\bm{M}\bm{Q}+\bm{Q}\bm{M}\right) (D.8)

This single matrix equation defines a closed 2121-dimensional system that fully characterizes learning in the rank-2 linear RNN and makes explicit how the loss-invisible entries of 𝑸\bm{Q} shape the evolution of its loss-visible entries. To validate this derivation, we train the rank-2 RNN to emulate the response of a second-order filter (damped sinusoidal [25]):

y⋆​(t)=e−c⋆​t​cos⁡(ω⋆​t)y^{\star}(t)=e^{-c^{\star}t}\cos(\omega^{\star}t) (D.9)

This target filter represents an oscillatory dynamics with frequency ω⋆\omega^{\star} and damping rate c⋆c^{\star} (set to 2 and 0.3, respectively). Aside from initializing the RNN with rank-2 connectivity, all simulation details remain identical to those used in the rank-1 analysis App. A.4.1. Numerically training a high-dimensional RNN on this task, we find that both the loss and overlap trajectories align perfectly with the predictions of our scalar ODE system. This demonstrates the generality of our derivation beyond the rank-1 case (Fig. 13).

Note

For a general rank-rr architecture with multiple inputs 𝒎in\bm{m}_{\text{in}} and outputs 𝒛out\bm{z}_{\text{out}}, the derivation follows the same logic: define the full set of pairwise overlaps and apply the chain rule to obtain their induced dynamics. In this general case, the total number of overlaps—both loss-visible and loss-invisible—scales as 𝒪⁡((2​r+𝒎in+𝒛out)2)\mathcal{O}((2r+\bm{m}_{\text{in}}+\bm{z}_{\text{out}})^{2}). While this expression grows quadratically with the rank and the number of input/output channels, it remains strictly independent of the network size NN. In this sense, the resulting dynamics remain tractable.
